title: Part 2, Chapter 52
paragraphs: Which relates the adventure of the second distressed or afflicted duenna, otherwise known as Doña Rodriguez

Cide Hamete tells us that Don Quixote, now healed of his scratches, decided that the life he was living in the castle ran completely against the order of chivalry he professed, so he resolved to ask the duke and duchess for permission to leave for Saragossa, since the festival there was approaching and he hoped to win the suit of armor that is awarded as the prize at tournaments of that kind. But one day, while he sat at table with the duke and duchess and was on the point of acting on his resolution and asking their leave, suddenly there came through the door of the great hall two women — for so they later proved to be — dressed in mourning from head to foot. One of them came up to Don Quixote and threw herself full length at his feet, pressing her lips against them and letting out moans so sad, so deep, and so mournful that everyone who heard and saw her was left bewildered. The duke and duchess assumed it must be some prank their servants were playing on Don Quixote, yet the earnestness with which the woman sighed, moaned, and wept perplexed them and left them in doubt, until Don Quixote, moved by pity, lifted her up and asked her to unveil herself and draw the mantle away from her tear-stained face. She did so, and revealed something nobody could possibly have expected, for she uncovered the face of Doña Rodriguez, the duenna of the household; the other woman in mourning was her daughter, the girl who had been deceived by the rich farmer's son. Everyone who knew her was astonished, and the duke and duchess most of all, for though they considered her a simpleton and a feeble creature, they had never believed her capable of such mad escapades. At last Doña Rodriguez turned to her master and mistress and said to them, "Would your excellences kindly allow me to speak with this gentleman for a moment? I must do so if I am to come out successfully from a business into which the insolence of an ill-intentioned peasant has dragged me."
The duke replied that for his part she had his permission, and that she could talk with Señor Don Quixote as long as she pleased.

Then, turning toward Don Quixote and speaking directly to him, she said, "Some days ago, valiant knight, I told you about the wrong and the treachery a wicked farmer has done to my dearly beloved daughter — the unfortunate girl standing here before you — and you promised me to take up her cause and set right the injury done to her. But now word has reached me that you mean to leave this castle in search of whatever good adventures God may grant you; and so, before you set out on the road, I ask that you challenge this insolent rustic and force him to marry my daughter, in keeping with the promise he made to be her husband before he seduced her. To expect my lord the duke to give me justice is to ask the elm tree for pears, for the reason I explained to your worship in private. And with that, may our Lord grant you good health and never abandon us."

Don Quixote answered these words with great gravity and solemnity: "Worthy duenna, hold back your tears — or rather, dry them — and save your sighs, for I take it upon myself to win redress for your daughter, though it would have gone better for her had she not been so quick to trust lovers' promises, which are mostly made in a moment and kept very slowly. So, with my lord the duke's permission, I will set out at once to find this heartless young man, and I will track him down and challenge him and kill him if he refuses to keep his pledged word; for the chief purpose of my profession is to spare the humble and punish the proud — I mean, to aid the distressed and crush the oppressors."

"There is no need," said the duke, "for your worship to go to the trouble of hunting down the rustic this good duenna complains of, nor is there any need to ask my permission to challenge him; for I declare him duly challenged, and I will see to it that he is told of the challenge, that he accepts it, and that he comes to answer it in person here at this castle of mine, where I will provide a fair field for both of you, observing all the conditions that are customarily and rightly observed in trials of this kind, and dealing justly with both sides, as every prince who grants combatants a free field within the bounds of his domain is obliged to do."

"Then with that assurance, and with your highness's kind permission," said Don Quixote, "I hereby, for this occasion, renounce my privilege of gentle birth and lower myself to the level of the offender's humble station, making myself his equal and so entitling him to meet me in combat. And therefore I challenge and defy him, absent though he is, on the grounds of the wrong he did in breaking faith with this poor damsel, who was a maiden and through his misdeed is one no longer; and I declare that he must keep the promise he gave to become her lawful husband, or else stake his life on the issue."

Then, pulling off a glove, he flung it down in the middle of the hall, and the duke picked it up, repeating what he had said before — that he accepted the challenge in his vassal's name. He set the date six days from then, the castle courtyard as the place, and for weapons the usual arms of knights: lance and shield and full armor, with all the rest of the equipment, free of trickery, fraud, or charms of any kind, and inspected and approved by the judges of the field. "But first of all," he said, "this worthy duenna and this unworthy damsel must place their claim for justice in the hands of Don Quixote; otherwise nothing can proceed, and the challenge cannot be carried to a lawful conclusion."
"I do so place it," the duenna replied.
"And so do I," added her daughter, weeping and overcome with shame and confusion.

Once this declaration had been made, and the duke had settled in his own mind how he would handle the affair, the women in black withdrew, and the duchess gave orders that from then on they were not to be treated as servants of hers but as lady adventurers who had come to her house seeking justice. So they were given a room of their own and waited on as though they were strangers, to the alarm of the other women-servants, who could not imagine where the foolishness and recklessness of Doña Rodriguez and her unlucky daughter would end.

And now, to round off the celebration and bring the dinner to a happy close, who should walk into the hall but the page who had carried the letters and presents to Teresa Panza, wife of the governor Sancho. The duke and duchess were delighted to see him, eager to hear how his journey had gone; but when they asked him, the page answered that he could not report it in front of so many people or in a few words, and he begged their excellences to let it wait for a private moment and to entertain themselves with these letters in the meantime; and taking out the letters, he placed them in the duchess's hands. One bore as its address, _Letter for my lady the Duchess So-and-so, of I don't know where_; the other, _To my husband Sancho Panza, governor of the island of Barataria, whom God prosper longer than me_. The duchess's bread would not bake, as the saying goes, until she had read her letter; and after glancing over it herself and seeing it was fit to be read aloud for the duke and everyone present to hear, she read out as follows.
TERESA PANZA'S LETTER TO THE DUCHESS.

The letter your highness wrote me, my lady, gave me great pleasure, for truly it was very welcome. The string of coral beads is very fine, and my husband's hunting suit is every bit its match. The whole village is delighted that your ladyship has made my good man Sancho a governor, though nobody will believe it — least of all the curate, and Master Nicholas the barber, and the bachelor Samson Carrasco; but I don't mind that, for as long as it's true, which it is, they can all say whatever they please. Though to be honest, if the coral beads and the suit hadn't arrived, I wouldn't have believed it either; for everyone in this village takes my husband for a blockhead, and apart from governing a herd of goats they can't imagine what sort of government he could be fit for. God grant it, and guide him as he sees his children have need. With your worship's leave, lady of my soul, I've made up my mind to make the most of this fine day and go to Court, to stretch out at my ease in a coach and make all those who already envy me burst their eyes out. So I beg your excellence to order my husband to send me a small trifle of money — and let it be enough to mention — because expenses run high at Court: a loaf costs a real, and meat is thirty maravedis a pound, which is past all bearing. And if he doesn't want me to go, let him tell me in good time, for my feet are itching to be off; and my friends and neighbors tell me that if my daughter and I cut a fine figure and make a brave show at Court, my husband will come to be known through me far more than I through him, for naturally plenty of people will ask, "Who are those ladies in that coach?" and some servant of mine will answer, "The wife and daughter of Sancho Panza, governor of the island of Barataria;" and that way Sancho will become known, and I'll be well thought of, and "to Rome for everything." I am as annoyed as can be that no acorns were gathered in our village this year; even so I'm sending your highness about half a peck of them, which I went to the wood to gather and picked out one by one myself, and I couldn't find any bigger; I wish they were the size of ostrich eggs. Don't let your high mightiness forget to write to me, and I'll be sure to answer and tell you how I am and whatever news there is in this place, where I remain, praying our Lord to keep your highness in his care and not to forget me. Sancha my daughter and my son kiss your worship's hands. She who would rather see your ladyship than write to you,
Your humble servant, TERESA PANZA.

Everyone was greatly entertained by Teresa Panza's letter, especially the duke and duchess; and the duchess asked Don Quixote whether, in his opinion, they might open the letter addressed to the governor, which she suspected must be excellent. Don Quixote said that to please them he would open it himself, and he did so, and found that it read as follows.
TERESA PANZA'S LETTER TO HER HUSBAND SANCHO PANZA.

I received thy letter, Sancho of my soul, and I promise thee and swear as a Catholic Christian that I came within two fingers' breadth of going mad, I was so happy. Believe me, brother, when I heard that thou wert a governor I thought I'd drop down dead from sheer joy — and thou knowest the saying that sudden joy can kill as surely as great sorrow; as for Sanchica thy daughter, she wet herself from pure happiness. There I stood with the suit thou hadst sent me before me, and my lady the duchess's coral beads around my neck, and the letters in my hands, with the man who brought them standing right there, and even so I truly believed and thought that everything I was seeing and touching was a dream; for who could have imagined that a goatherd would end up governor of islands? Thou knowest, my friend, what my mother used to say: one must live long to see much. I say it because I expect to see more if I live longer, for I don't mean to stop until I see thee a tax-farmer or a collector of revenue — offices where, though the devil carries off those who abuse them, the holders always make and handle money. My lady the duchess will tell thee how much I long to go to Court; think it over and let me know thy pleasure; I'll try to do thee credit by traveling in a coach. Neither the curate, nor the barber, nor the bachelor, nor even the sacristan can believe thou art a governor; they say the whole business is a delusion or some enchantment affair, like everything to do with thy master Don Quixote; and Samson says he means to go and find thee and drive the government out of thy head and the madness out of Don Quixote's skull. I just laugh and look at my string of beads and plan the dress I'm going to make for our daughter out of thy suit. I sent some acorns to my lady the duchess; I wish they had been gold. Send me a few strings of pearls, if they're in fashion on that island. Here is the village news: La Berrueca has married her daughter to a good-for-nothing painter who came here to paint whatever turned up. The council hired him to paint his Majesty's arms over the door of the town hall; he asked two ducats, which they paid him in advance; he worked for eight days, and at the end of them had painted nothing, and then said he had no knack for painting such trifles. He gave back the money, yet for all that he has married on the strength of being a good craftsman — though it's true he has now put down his paintbrush and taken up a spade, and goes out to the fields like a gentleman. Pedro Lobo's son has taken first orders and the tonsure, meaning to become a priest. Minguilla, Mingo Silvato's granddaughter, found out about it and has gone to law with him, claiming he promised to marry her. Wicked tongues say she is carrying his child, but he flatly denies it. There are no olives this year, and there isn't a drop of vinegar to be found in the whole village. A company of soldiers passed through; when they left they took three of the village girls with them. I won't tell thee who they are; perhaps they'll come back, and there are sure to be men who'll take them as wives, blemishes and all, for better or worse. Sanchica is making bonelace; she clears eight maravedis a day, which she drops into a moneybox toward setting up house; but now that she's a governor's daughter, thou wilt give her a dowry without her having to work for it. The fountain in the plaza has run dry. Lightning struck the gibbet — and may every bolt land there, for all I care. I'll be waiting for an answer to this, and for thy decision about my going to Court; and so, may God keep thee longer than me, or as long, for I would not want to leave thee in this world without me.
Your wife, TERESA PANZA.

The letters were applauded, laughed over, savored, and admired; and then, as if to set the seal on the whole business, the courier arrived carrying the letter Sancho had sent to Don Quixote. This too was read aloud, and it cast some doubt on the governor's supposed simplicity. The duchess withdrew to hear from the page what had happened to him in Sancho's village, and he told her everything at full length without leaving out a single detail. He gave her the acorns, along with a cheese Teresa had sent as being especially good — better than the cheeses of Tronchon. The duchess received it with the greatest delight, and there we shall leave her, in order to describe how the government of the great Sancho Panza, flower and mirror of all governors of islands, came to its end.
